title: Facing Islamophobia
hook: prejudice against Muslims, and how communities respond with patience and openness

segments.voice: Yesterday, interfaith friendship, and a letter built on two commandments. Your line was love of God and neighbor. Did you ask your question, and hear the whole answer? Today, the neighbor who doesn't want to know you. Day one thousand three hundred ninety.

A note taped to a mosque door overnight. Ugly words, misspelled, telling the people inside to go home, when this is home. The imam finds it before dawn prayer. What happens next is a choice. Some mosques that have faced moments like this have answered by opening the doors wider: an open day, tea in the hall, a sign that says come in and ask us anything. It isn't the only answer, and it isn't easy. Today, facing Islamophobia, and an old story about the hardest day.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE DOOR.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?` → `THE DOORS OPEN WIDER.`

segments.voice: Islamophobia is the word people use for prejudice and hostility toward Muslims, and toward people taken to be Muslim because of a name, a beard or a headscarf. It can be a shout on a bus, a vandalized wall, or a door that quietly stays closed at a job interview. The tradition has its own memory of rejection. In Sahih al-Bukhari, 'A'ishah once asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, whether he ever had a day harder than the battle of Uhud. He says yes, and tells her about a day he went to a man of standing to ask for support, and was turned away. He walked off so grieved, he says, that he hardly knew where he was until he reached a place on the road. Then an angel of the mountains came and offered to bring the two mountains down on the town. And he said no. He hoped, instead, that from their descendants would come people who worship God alone. The Qur'an puts the principle in Surah Fussilat, in Pickthall: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better." And it goes on: the one who was your enemy may become like a close friend. In Surah al-Furqan, the servants of the Merciful are described as those who, when the ignorant address them, answer: peace. That's the patience and openness in today's line. But patience isn't the same as silence. Communities also document what happens, report it, and turn to the law. The Prophet's answer that day wasn't to pretend nothing had happened. It was to refuse to answer in kind, and keep a future open.
screen: `PREJUDICE TOWARD MUSLIMS.` · `THE HARDEST DAY: TURNED AWAY.` · `REPEL THE EVIL DEED WITH A BETTER ONE.` · `PATIENCE IS NOT SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse standing up for someone harassed. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a train, a store, a sidewalk. Someone is being shouted at for how they look or pray. You don't have to confront the shouter. Picture yourself walking over and standing beside the person being targeted. Say something ordinary to them: hi, are you okay, want to walk with me? Stay until it's over. Afterward, ask what they need. If you pray, you can hold that person in mind. If you don't, simply rehearse the first sentence until it's yours. The bell holds the time.
Facing Islamophobia. Prejudice against Muslims, met with patience, openness, and the refusal to answer in kind. Today's word.

Your line: answer hate with good. Today, if you see someone harassed, go stand beside them, and if you don't, learn how to report it where you live. Tomorrow, mental health and faith. Day one thousand three hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Muslim communities facing prejudice respond in different ways: some mosques hold open days and invite neighbors in, while community groups also document incidents, support those targeted, and work with the police and the courts.

original.note: Arabic: patience, steadfastness: holding firm without answering in kind.

trapdoor: what you thought: patience means letting people walk all over you.
what it means: refusing to answer hate in kind, keeping a future open, while still naming and reporting what happened.
what a scholar hears: the hardest day in al-Bukhari and the angel of the mountains; 41:34 on repelling evil with better; 25:63 on answering the ignorant with peace.

notes: Confirm Pickthall's wording for 41:34 exactly as quoted.

Bukhari 3231: the town is commonly identified as Ta'if and the day as the visit to Ibn 'Abd Yalil; the script does not name the town or say he was stoned, since the report itself doesn't. Confirm the retelling.

The hook's note on a mosque door is an illustrative scenario, not a reported event. 'Some mosques that have faced moments like this have answered by opening the doors wider' is general and unsourced; a Keeper may add a named example.
Practice describes a bystander approach (stand beside the person targeted, don't confront the harasser); confirm it is appropriate and safe as written.
The original game uses sabr (patience), which is not the day's word but names the outline's 'patience'.
Editor: the report in Bukhari 3231 has him present himself to one man (Ibn 'Abd Yalil), not to 'a town's leaders'; the teach now says 'a man of standing'.
